title: Arithmetic Progression Class 11 (CBSE): nth Term, Sum & Solved Problems + Quiz
meta_title: Arithmetic Progression Class 11 CBSE: Formulas + Quiz
meta_desc: Master Class 11 Arithmetic Progression the CBSE way: nth term a+(n-1)d, sum of n terms, arithmetic mean, solved problems and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: An AP is just a list of numbers that climbs (or falls) by the same step each time. Get two formulas straight and most CBSE questions fall over. Here is the concept, the problem types the exam actually asks, and a quiz to test yourself.
content:
Arithmetic progression is one of the friendliest chapters in Class 11 — two formulas do almost all the heavy lifting — yet it quietly trips up students in the board exam because they memorise the formulas without ever pinning down what a, d and n actually stand for. Get those three straight and the rest is careful substitution.

An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number to the one before it. That fixed number is the common difference, written d. So 3, 7, 11, 15, … is an AP with first term a = 3 and d = 4. The quickest test: subtract any term from the one after it. If you always get the same answer, it is an AP. For 3, 7, 11 that check gives 7 − 3 = 4 and 11 − 7 = 4, so d = 4 throughout.

Note that d can be negative (the sequence falls, as in 20, 17, 14, …) or zero (every term is the same). That single sign catches out more students in the exam than any formula does.

The nth term of an AP

Rather than list out fifty terms to find the fiftieth, we jump straight to it. The nth term (also called the general term) is

an = a + (n − 1)d

The logic is worth seeing once. The first term is a with zero steps added; the second term is a + one d; the third is a + two d. So the nth term is a plus (n − 1) lots of d — you always take one step fewer than the term number. That ‘n − 1, not n’ is the single most common slip in this chapter.

Say a company’s starting salary is Rs 25,000 with an annual raise of Rs 2,000. The salary in year 10 is a10 = 25000 + (10 − 1)(2000) = 25000 + 18000 = Rs 43,000. No listing required.

Sum of n terms

The famous story is that a young Gauss added 1 to 100 in seconds by pairing 1 with 100, 2 with 99, and so on — fifty pairs each summing to 101. That pairing trick is exactly what the sum formula encodes. The sum of the first n terms is

Sn = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d]

When you already know the last term l, a neater version works:

Sn = n/2 × (a + l)

Read that second form as ‘number of terms, times the average of the first and last term’. It is Gauss’s pairing written as algebra. Use the (a + l) version whenever the last term is handed to you, and the [2a + (n − 1)d] version when it is not — picking the right one saves a line of working under exam pressure.

Arithmetic mean

If three numbers are in AP, the middle one is the arithmetic mean (AM) of the other two. Concretely, the AM of two numbers p and q is (p + q)/2, and inserting it between them gives a three-term AP. CBSE often extends this: ‘insert k arithmetic means between two numbers’ simply means build an AP with those two numbers at the ends and k equally spaced terms in between, which you handle by finding d from an = a + (n − 1)d.

Problem types CBSE keeps asking

The chapter recycles a handful of setups. Recognise the type and you already know the first move.

  • Find a specific term: given a and d, plug into an = a + (n − 1)d.
  • Two conditions, two unknowns: ‘the 4th term is 11 and the 7th term is 20’ gives two equations in a and d. Subtract them to kill a and get d in one step.
  • How many terms / which term equals a value: set an equal to the value and solve for n. If n is not a whole number, the value is not in the AP.
  • Sum problems: spot whether you are given the last term (use n/2(a + l)) or not (use the full formula).
  • Three numbers in AP: take them as (a − d), a, (a + d). Their sum is 3a, which collapses the algebra beautifully.

A worked two-condition problem

Suppose the 4th term of an AP is 11 and the 7th term is 20. Then a + 3d = 11 and a + 6d = 20. Subtracting the first from the second gives 3d = 9, so d = 3, and back-substitution gives a = 2. The AP is 2, 5, 8, 11, … That subtract-to-eliminate move is the workhorse of the whole chapter.

Common mistakes to avoid

Three errors account for most lost marks. First, using n instead of (n − 1) in the nth-term formula — always take one step fewer than the term number. Second, mishandling a negative common difference; when the sequence falls, d is negative and must stay negative all the way through. Third, mixing up the two sum formulas — check whether the question hands you the last term before you decide which to use. A fourth, subtler one: assuming a sequence is an AP without testing that the difference is truly constant. Always verify with two or three consecutive differences first.

Test yourself

Below is a free 8-question quiz pitched at exactly Class 11 CBSE level — nth term, sum of n terms, arithmetic mean and the two-condition setup. Attempt each one on paper, then read the explanation for anything you miss. If a whole type keeps catching you out, that is the section to revise before your next test.

quiz.title: Class 11 Arithmetic Progression Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions covering the nth term, sum of n terms, arithmetic mean and two-condition problems. Work each on paper, choose an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: For the AP 5, 8, 11, 14, ..., what is the common difference d?
questions.explanation: Subtract any term from the next: 8 - 5 = 3 and 11 - 8 = 3, so d = 3.

questions.q: What is the 15th term of the AP with a = 2 and d = 4?
questions.explanation: a15 = a + (n - 1)d = 2 + (15 - 1)(4) = 2 + 56 = 58. Remember it is 14 steps, not 15.

questions.q: The sum of the first n natural numbers 1 + 2 + ... + n is:
questions.explanation: This is an AP with a = 1, l = n, so Sn = n/2 (a + l) = n(n + 1)/2 - the Gauss pairing formula.

questions.q: The arithmetic mean of 12 and 30 is:
In an AP the 4th term is 11 and the 7th term is 20. What is the common difference?
questions.explanation: a + 3d = 11 and a + 6d = 20. Subtracting gives 3d = 9, so d = 3.

questions.q: Which term of the AP 3, 7, 11, 15, ... equals 43?
What is the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 2, 5, 8, 11, ...?
For the AP 20, 17, 14, 11, ..., what is the 6th term?
questions.explanation: Here d = -3 (the sequence falls). a6 = 20 + (6 - 1)(-3) = 20 - 15 = 5. Keep d negative throughout.

faq.q: What is an arithmetic progression in Class 11?
faq.a: An arithmetic progression is a sequence where each term after the first is found by adding a fixed number, the common difference d, to the previous term. For example 3, 7, 11, 15 is an AP with d = 4. The two core formulas are the nth term a + (n - 1)d and the sum of n terms n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d].

faq.q: How do I find the nth term of an AP?
faq.a: Use a_n = a + (n - 1)d, where a is the first term, d is the common difference and n is the term number. The most common mistake is using n instead of (n - 1) - you always add one step fewer than the term number, because the first term has no steps added.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two sum formulas?
faq.a: Use Sn = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] when you know the first term and common difference. Use the shorter Sn = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is given, since it is simply the number of terms times the average of the first and last term. Both give the same answer.

faq.q: What is arithmetic mean in an AP?
faq.a: If three numbers are in AP, the middle one is the arithmetic mean of the other two. For two numbers p and q the arithmetic mean is (p + q)/2. Inserting it between them creates a three-term AP, which is why 'insert k arithmetic means' questions are just building an AP with those numbers at the ends.

faq.q: How can I practise Class 11 AP problems?
faq.a: Start with the 8-question quiz above - it covers the nth term, sum of n terms, arithmetic mean and two-condition problems at CBSE level, with a worked explanation for every answer. Attempt each on paper first, then check your reasoning against the explanation to find exactly which type needs more work.
